Week 93 Appendix: The Week the Clock Held Its Breath

DOJ waged an unprecedented legal siege on a national election while courts, officials, and voters refused to yield ground.

This was a week in which the executive branch mounted the most direct and sustained assault yet on the machinery of a specific election, using DOJ lawsuits, subpoenas, fabricated noncitizen-voter claims, and threats of prosecution against state and local election officials in California, Washington, Alaska, and beyond—all in the days before the midterms. Courts in multiple instances (Ninth Circuit, federal district judges) rebuffed these efforts, providing a partial institutional check, but the pattern itself—conditioning lawsuits on which party wins, a $1 million fraud bounty, and calls to prosecute and remove a sitting candidate—signals a White House treating electoral outcomes as negotiable. Simultaneously, a House Judiciary report escalated allegations of presidential sexual assault tied to Epstein and alleged DOJ obstruction, while Brazil's democratic transition (Lula's win, Bolsonaro's flight, and US sheltering of his son) tied domestic and international democratic erosion together.

Power and Authority

  1. Trump waived sanctions on Russian energy company Novatek to enable Alaska LNG deal: The president waived congressionally mandated sanctions on a Putin-linked firm two days before they took effect, undermining separation of powers and inviting foreign financial entanglement. (2026-10-24)
  2. Hegseth and Rubio signed Venezuelan oil venture agreement with money-laundering-accused oligarch: Cabinet secretaries signed a resource-extraction deal via an offshore shell structure with a figure accused of money laundering, raising conflict-of-interest and oversight concerns. (2026-10-24)
  3. Trump administration sued Alaska to block Senate election certification: DOJ sued to preemptively block certification of a Senate race the incumbent might lose, treating an electoral loss as grounds for federal intervention before any results existed. (2026-10-24)
  4. Trump administration requested CISA hack voting machines early in term: DHS appointees reportedly asked the election-security agency to secretly hack a voting machine and report findings to the White House, a request that alarmed career staff as improper interference. (2026-10-24)
  5. Obama criticized White House renovations at Ohio rally: A former president publicly mocked the administration's spending on White House renovations, injecting fiscal-priority criticism into midterm campaigning. (2026-10-25)
  6. Trump dismissed concerns about high gas prices at Georgia rally: The president dismissed public hardship from fuel costs while touting record profits, reflecting on administration priorities regarding economic burden on ordinary citizens. (2026-10-25)
  7. Trump demanded Representative Omar resign and falsely claimed she conceded her seat: The president made a false public claim that a sitting member of Congress had conceded her seat, undermining the legitimacy of elected representation. (2026-10-26)
  8. Justice Department announced charges involving 48 aliens for election-related crimes: DOJ publicized criminal charges against noncitizens for alleged voting violations across five states, amplifying fraud narratives ahead of the midterms. (2026-10-26)
  9. Trump administration enacted largest federal healthcare cut in U.S. history via budget legislation: A roughly $1 trillion reduction to Medicaid funding threatens hospital closures and access to care for low-income Americans, striking at the social safety net. (2026-10-27) [single source]
  10. White House evaluated blanket pardons for junior staff: Consideration of mass pardons for staff would remove incentives to cooperate with investigations and shield potential wrongdoing from accountability. (2026-10-27) [single source]
  11. National Labor Relations Board closed Memphis subregional office, consolidating service to other cities: Closure of a regional labor-rights office reduces field capacity for workers seeking protection against unfair labor practices in a multi-state area. (2026-10-29)
  12. Trump called for Peltola's removal from ballot and prosecution: The president called for a political opponent to be removed from the ballot and prosecuted over a legal campaign tactic, equating ordinary politics with criminal fraud. (2026-10-29)
  13. Trump directed DOJ to sue to block Alaska Senate election certification: The president personally ordered litigation to block certification of an election outcome contingent on his preferred candidate losing, striking at the peaceful transfer of power. (2026-10-30)
  14. Trump ordered State Department to grant Flávio Bolsonaro temporary humanitarian status: The president personally directed immigration relief for a foreign political figure fleeing accountability after an electoral defeat, signaling support for anti-democratic actors abroad. (2026-10-30)
  15. Justice Department announced final rule allowing voluntary NICS use for employee background checks: DOJ finalized a rule enabling firearms licensees to voluntarily screen employees through the national background-check system, expanding use of a federal database. (2026-10-30)
  16. Justice Department announced issuance of federal registrations for medical marijuana dispensaries: DEA began issuing federal registrations to state-licensed dispensaries under a reclassification policy, reshaping the federal-state regulatory relationship on cannabis. (2026-10-30)
  17. Justice Department announced $300 million in awards to four cities to combat violent crime: DOJ directed federal funding toward local policing initiatives under a public-safety program, shaping local law-enforcement priorities through federal money. (2026-10-30)
  18. White House adjusted tariffs on robotics and industrial machinery imports: The president issued a proclamation altering import rules for robotics and machinery, exercising unilateral trade authority with broad economic effects. (2026-10-28)
